1.name: Ameer Young
1.bio: Young put together high-level tape at Missouri before taking over at Clemson and winning the Heisman. He brings the experience of leading two college offenses across five seasons and the command to operate at the center of a passing game. His track record gives a franchise an elite quarterback prospect.

2.name: Michael Oluwafemi
2.bio: Oluwafemi makes the extraordinary look like part of the weekly routine. Washington’s generational receiver turned his final college season into a showcase, overwhelming defenses with production and playmaking. His complete skill set has evaluators projecting a top-tier NFL receiver from day one.

13.name: LaMarian Johnson
13.bio: Johnson makes the first defender miss, then has the balance to keep the run alive. South Carolina’s powerful back combines vision and athleticism with elite tackle-breaking ability, creating the kind of production that can make a ground game run through him.

15.name: DaQuan Battles
15.bio: Battles turns contact into another opportunity to gain ground. The Ohio State runner brings power and a knack for breaking tackles, keeping his legs moving through traffic and piling up yards after contact. His presence gives a backfield a forceful identity.

19.name: Dejon Stokes
19.bio: Stokes gives Michigan a runner who can change the shape of a play in a hurry. His vision and soft hands make him a threat out of the backfield, while his ability to break long gains adds another dimension to an offense.

25.name: Armani Johnson
25.bio: Sharing an Ohio State backfield hasn’t kept Johnson from drawing first-round attention. The big runner has the size to handle a substantial workload and the elusiveness to make defenders miss in space, giving teams another standout option in a deep class.

28.name: Jordan Ruiz
28.bio: Ruiz can make a crowded middle of the field feel wide open. Penn State’s polished slot receiver pairs elite route running with soft hands, giving his quarterback a reliable target and an offense a prospect capable of growing into a dangerous second option.

31.name: Maxx DiMarco
31.bio: DiMarco protects the football and gives Syracuse a credible rushing threat when the pocket changes shape. His arm opens passing options, and his mobility gives the offense another way to move the chains. That combination gives a professional team several ways to use him at quarterback.

33.name: Brayan Williams
33.bio: Williams gives Alabama a tight end who can make the middle of the field uncomfortable. His athleticism and ability to attack the seam create opportunities beyond the underneath routes, giving a quarterback a receiving threat who can challenge coverage vertically.

34.name: Dillan Jones
34.bio: The ball rarely escapes Jones once it reaches his hands. The Illinois transfer brings the best hands in the class to Oregon, along with good speed and underrated playmaking ability. His blend of reliability and movement gives a passing game room to get creative.

37.name: Johnathan Ragland
37.bio: Ragland has the athletic ability to make his college production look like only part of the story. The highly recruited Miami receiver offers a lean frame and promising movement skills; his projection rests on converting that talent into more consistent professional production.

38.name: Rontay Jenkins
38.bio: Jenkins transferred from Georgia Tech to Tennessee and brings rare arm strength that invites comparisons to Josh Allen. He can make throws most prospects cannot attempt. The rest of his game needs polish, and his projection depends on becoming a more dependable passer from snap to snap.

40.name: Marquavious Keys
40.bio: Keys needs only a sliver of space to make a defender miss. Oklahoma’s compact receiver combines elite speed with a devastating juke, turning touches into open-field threats. His smaller catch radius makes accurate placement important, but the payoff arrives once the ball is secured.

42.name: Zion Ellis
42.bio: Ellis arrives with plenty of football still ahead of him. The young Georgia back has relatively little wear from a limited workload and brings elite talent in a smaller package, giving an offense an exciting foundation to develop in its backfield.

44.name: J.C. Reiter
44.bio: Reiter has a way of making a difficult throw look safe. Cincinnati’s tight end brings exceptionally soft hands and the athleticism to slip behind linebackers, giving his quarterback a dependable target with more downfield potential than his reputation might suggest.

45.name: Jay Maxwell
45.bio: Maxwell makes himself an easy choice when a quarterback needs an answer. Stanford’s athletic tight end produced strong numbers and substantial yardage per catch, using his movement to make plays downfield despite a smaller frame than many players at the position.

50.name: Brian Soto
50.bio: Soto found his rhythm at Penn State and kept it throughout his final season. The tight end developed into a consistent receiving option from start to finish, offering his quarterback a dependable presence and giving evaluators a full season of established production.

52.name: Isaiah Abraham-Jenkins
52.bio: Inside the red zone, Abraham-Jenkins gives his quarterback a target who can rise above the crowd. Michigan’s big receiver turned limited yardage into touchdown production and occasional chunk plays. His size and downfield ability give an offense a clear scoring weapon.

61.name: Mohammed Ekwueme
61.bio: Ekwueme brings a big frame and a punishing style to Oregon after transferring from Washington. The power back builds momentum as he carries the ball, giving a defense an increasingly difficult assignment when an offense commits to the ground game.

64.name: Tre Miles
64.bio: Miles brings a receiver’s background and rare movement skills to Georgia’s tight end group. The former wideout is the most athletic player at the position in this class, giving an offense a vertical threat who can stretch coverage and create matchup problems.

76.name: Terrelle McDonald
76.bio: McDonald looks like a receiver and brings the hands to match. Memphis can use him out of the backfield, while his ability to slip through narrow openings gives him value as a runner. His receiving skill set offers a clear professional role.

80.name: Noah Lorenz
80.bio: Lorenz has a habit of finding open grass when his quarterback needs it. North Dakota State’s older tight end became the offense’s top option despite a modest athletic profile, using his understanding of space to consistently present a clean throwing window.

82.name: Mike Keeney
82.bio: Keeney gives Michigan an inline tight end built for a physical offense. His blocking fits a run-heavy scheme, while reliable hands, size and a large catch radius give his quarterback an inviting target when the offense turns to the passing game.

85.name: David Gonzalez
85.bio: Gonzalez gives Ole Miss a back who can contribute throughout the offense. The former five-star recruit pairs soft hands with a consistent knack for creating big plays, offering the kind of versatility that can keep defenses guessing when he touches the ball.

91.name: Matt Delaney
91.bio: Delaney transferred from UNLV and capably filled the USC job after J.T. Rhoads departed. His time running that offense supports a projection as a backup who can make spot starts. The question is whether he can build on that steady play over a longer assignment.

92.name: Talon Winston IV
92.bio: Winston brings the kind of speed that forces a defense to account for him before the snap. The slight Florida State receiver pairs soft hands with elite agility and can take touches from the backfield, giving an offense several ways to manufacture space.

94.name: Zahair Blackwell
94.bio: Blackwell brings track speed and creativity to the Georgia Tech backfield. The compact gadget threat can make defenders miss in the open field and turn a small crease into a long gain, making designed touches a natural way to use his ability.

98.name: Imanif Ali
98.bio: Arizona State’s Ali enters the class as a 6-foot-2 safety with a versatile defensive role. His profile gives evaluators a chance to consider how his frame can fit across the back end, from deep assignments to responsibilities closer to the line.

99.name: Evan Brown
99.bio: Brown gives Texas a 6-foot-3 edge defender for scouts to evaluate along the right side of the front. His pass-rush role puts him in the conversation for teams looking at where an outside defender fits and how he can contribute in their defensive rotation.

100.name: Derick Soliz
100.bio: Soliz gives Washington a 6-foot-5 possession receiver whose size opens up throws near the goal line. He can use his frame to give the quarterback a target when coverage tightens. His acceleration is limited, so his best opportunities come when the route rewards positioning and reach.

101.name: Jake Fulton
101.bio: Fulton has the build and arm profile to develop as a backup with a chance to grow into a starting role. The Oklahoma State senior needs to produce more high-impact throws. That improvement would give evaluators more evidence that his tools can carry a larger workload.

102.name: Will Hoggard
102.bio: Hoggard showed flashes at Stanford, but there were more difficult stretches than strong ones across the season. Too many plays put the ball in danger. His clearest path forward is to reduce those decisions and give an offense more dependable play between the occasional highs.

103.name: Dan Rudnick
103.bio: Rudnick has the size teams look for in a quarterback, and he puts it to use as a runner. The Duke senior can break tackles and extend rushing plays through contact. His passing traits are more ordinary, so that running value is central to his projection.

104.name: Jackson Beckett
104.bio: Beckett put together productive passing numbers at Western Kentucky by getting the ball out quickly. That timing helps him make the most of an arm with below-average strength. His game projects best when he can make the read early and deliver before the throwing window narrows.

105.name: Jordy Willis
105.bio: Willis brings a good arm and real speed in a compact frame, giving Georgia Tech a quarterback who can change the pace of a game. The next step is translating those tools into steadier quarterback play, especially when the offense needs him to sustain a drive.

106.name: Tyler Costa
106.bio: Costa fits the physical profile at 6-foot-5 and has a good arm to work with. The Utah State quarterback completed fewer than 58 percent of his passes, which puts accuracy at the center of his evaluation. More reliable ball placement could make those tools play up.

107.name: Matthew Christian
107.bio: Christian brings Indiana a 240-pound runner who can get downhill quickly and finish through contact. He keeps moving when defenders meet him square and can make a narrow interior lane pay off. His lateral agility limits his options when the initial crease closes and the play calls for a redirect.

108.name: Carter Johnson
108.bio: Johnson gives Oklahoma State an unusual blend of size and elusiveness. At 238 pounds, he can change direction and make a defender miss without giving up the frame of a larger back. That combination gives him a chance to handle work across all three downs.

109.name: Damien McMillan
109.bio: McMillan gets north quickly and uses powerful strides to carry momentum through contact. Texas can lean on that direct style when the blocking creates a clear lane. Congested fronts give him fewer answers, especially when the first opening closes and he has to create a new path.

110.name: Kareem Mason
110.bio: Mason slips through narrow openings and stays balanced when defenders get a piece of him. The compact Buffalo back can turn a crowded play into a useful gain with those traits. His speed rarely separates him from pursuit over distance, so his best work comes closer to the line.

111.name: Keon Hill
111.bio: Hill can plant and burst away before defenders recover, giving Texas a runner who creates space with sharp direction changes. His acceleration makes a small crease worth attacking. Larger defenders can stop his momentum when they get square, so most of his value comes from making them miss.

112.name: Collin Richardson
112.bio: Richardson gives USC a reliable target out of the backfield and can contribute in several receiving situations. His hands give the passing game a dependable option when a play calls for the back to get involved. His value is clearer in space because he is less effective on interior carries.

113.name: Sean Lester-Patton
113.bio: Lester-Patton gets downhill and finishes runs with enough force to gain ground through contact. Rutgers can use that dependable approach when it needs a runner to take the available yards and finish the play. His acceleration limits how often a clean opening becomes an explosive gain.

114.name: Jeremiah McIntyre
114.bio: McIntyre stays on his feet through contact and can work through crowded interior runs for South Carolina. His balance gives him a chance to finish plays when defenders reach him early. More consistent lane recognition would help him reach the right crease and put that strength to better use.

115.name: Colten Shifflett
115.bio: Shifflett runs polished routes and looks comfortable when Colorado State asks him to get involved in the passing game. His receiving skills give him a clear role when he can catch the ball in space. Once defenders square him up, he rarely breaks through the tackle.

116.name: Jeremiah Barnett II
116.bio: Barnett brings Michigan a physical runner with long strides and the strength to finish short-yardage carries. He can build momentum when the lane lets him get moving. Tight spaces make it harder for him to change direction suddenly, so his best carries give him a direct path.

117.name: Jaden Woods
117.bio: Woods can press the perimeter and make sharp cuts once he sees an opening. Penn State can use his agility to test defenders who have to contain the edge. He sometimes commits before a block develops, which can take away the space his movement would otherwise help him exploit.

118.name: Latrelle Murphy
118.bio: Murphy uses a powerful lower body to move through contact on runs between the tackles. Oklahoma can put him to work when the play calls for a direct downhill finish. He has less burst in open space, so his strengths show up more often in traffic than on long runs.

119.name: Purcell Lawrence Jr
119.bio: Lawrence gives Arizona a 240-pound runner who can build momentum downhill and finish with force. His size makes him difficult to stop once he gets his legs moving. He runs tall through contact, so lowering his pads would help him carry more of that power into the collision.

120.name: Bryce Henry
120.bio: Henry brings Temple compact power that can fit short goal-line carries. He has the build to work through tight quarters and finish when there is little room to build speed. He offers less on extended runs, where his long speed gives pursuit a chance to close.

121.name: Dejerius Wheeler
121.bio: Wheeler can change direction more easily than his 228-pound build suggests, giving Toledo a runner who can adjust when the lane shifts. The burst through an opening varies from carry to carry. A quicker first step into the crease would help him get more from his agility.

122.name: LaDorian Williams
122.bio: Williams brings Alabama a strong frame and the physical running style to contribute in a rotation. He can carry through contact when the blocking gives him a clean read. Sharper footwork and quicker recognition of developing lanes would help him make those carries more consistent.

123.name: Dante Burrell
123.bio: Burrell changes direction fluidly and gives Notre Dame a runner who can find a cutback when the front flows away from it. He can make the move in traffic, but his acceleration through the opening varies. Getting back to speed sooner would make those cuts more productive.

124.name: Prince Matthews
124.bio: Matthews stays patient while his blocks develop and has the instincts to find space once he reaches the open field. Washington State can use his elusiveness when he has room to change direction. He has less strength through contact, which limits the gains he can create in crowded lanes.

125.name: Marques Cook
125.bio: Cook makes quick lateral cuts underneath, giving Clemson a way to turn short throws into gains in space. The compact receiver can get a defender leaning before he changes direction. His limited catch radius puts more pressure on ball placement, especially when coverage closes before the pass arrives.

126.name: De'Kavion Prescott
126.bio: Prescott combines a 225-pound frame with the long speed to threaten Tennessee’s opponents vertically. Once he gets into stride, he can force coverage to turn and run with him. More precise routes would help him use that speed when a deeper throw depends on timing and spacing.

127.name: Athumo Mweyambugu
127.bio: Mweyambugu gives Georgia Tech a 6-foot-5 target who can win catches at the boundary with a defender in position. His size and ability to finish contested throws give the quarterback a viable window outside. He has less quickness to separate, so body positioning is central to his game.

128.name: Robin Jefferson Jr.
128.bio: Jefferson’s footwork gives Arizona State a receiver who can change direction fluidly and create once a play reaches the open field. He can improvise around a defender with room to work. More physical coverage can disrupt his rhythm before he gets enough space to put those moves to use.

129.name: Terrell Washington
129.bio: Washington uses long strides to stretch coverage and tracks the ball well once it is in the air. Clemson can put both traits to work on vertical throws that let him build speed. His underneath routes are less consistent, leaving room to improve at shorter depths.

130.name: Amari Johns
130.bio: Johns keeps his balance when defenders make contact after the catch, giving South Florida a receiver who can squeeze extra yardage from a completion. He is most dangerous once the ball is secured. More consistent separation would help him get enough touches to make that strength matter.

131.name: Ja'Kobe Edwards
131.bio: Edwards gives Georgia a strong-handed boundary receiver who can handle physical play outside. His frame helps him hold his ground when a defender closes on the throw. He is less flexible entering breaks, which can make it harder to create space on routes that demand a quick change of direction.

132.name: Ian Sanders
132.bio: Sanders gives North Texas a vertical target with the size and speed to threaten a defender once he gets downfield. A clean release lets him build momentum on deeper routes. His work off the line varies, so a more reliable release would help him reach those opportunities.

133.name: Eric Mays
133.bio: Mays gives Oklahoma State a 6-foot-5 possession target who can reach throws outside a defender’s leverage. That catch radius offers a useful option when the quarterback has a narrow window. Slower short-area movement limits his separation, making positioning important when he works through crowded coverage.

134.name: Corey Edwards Jr
134.bio: Edwards reads coverage well from the slot and gives Purdue a dependable option when a play asks him to settle into space. His awareness helps him find a throwing window at the right time. He offers less explosive upside, so his clearest role comes on throws that reward timing.

135.name: Ja'Michael Abernathy
135.bio: Abernathy has the acceleration to threaten deep coverage and can get into his stride quickly for Stanford. His speed gives the offense a reason to stretch the field with him. More consistent tracking and hands would help him finish the downfield opportunities his movement creates.

136.name: Zaniel Branch
136.bio: Branch stays balanced through contact after the catch, giving Mississippi State a compact target who can keep a short play going. His playmaking is most apparent with the ball in his hands. Improving the detail in his routes would make him a more dependable option before it gets there.

137.name: Rodnell Knight
137.bio: Knight gets to his downfield speed more quickly than his 220-pound frame suggests. Wyoming can use his strength and stride on vertical routes when he has room to build momentum. Man coverage gives him trouble when a defender stays attached and forces him to create his own separation.

138.name: Hau'oli'oli Liko
138.bio: Liko gives California a 6-foot-4 athlete with the versatility to contribute in different receiving situations. His length and movement give the offense several ways to get him involved. More consistent receiving fundamentals would help him turn those physical tools into dependable play when the ball comes his way.

139.name: Deandre Traylor
139.bio: Traylor brings the speed to threaten vertically for Michigan, especially when he can get into his route without early contact. His lighter frame gives physical press corners a way to interrupt that start. A cleaner release against contact would let him put that speed to work more often.

140.name: Kevin Spears
140.bio: Spears can make defenders adjust with quick cuts on underneath touches, giving Memphis a receiver who can create in space after the catch. He is less dependable when contact arrives at the catch point. Stronger finishes would let him make more of the throws his movement helps earn.
